content: The potential reversibility of the disease or infection must be considered at all stages of communication. If post-elimination surveillance data indicate that the disease or infection has resurged beyond defined thresholds or has reappeared, this change in endemicity status will be documented in the Global Health Observatory and the Weekly Epidemiological Record. Member States are responsible for ensuring that surveillance data are made available to the World Health Organization (WHO). For certain diseases, Member States that have achieved elimination as a public health problem may later request verification of the elimination of transmission, provided that appropriate evidence supports this achievement. In the WHO South-East Asia Region, kala-azar (KA), also known as visceral leishmaniasis (VL), is predominantly endemic in Bangladesh, India, and Nepal, with sporadic cases reported in Bhutan and Thailand. In 2005, a program was initiated to eliminate KA as a public health problem, with a target of reducing the incidence to 1 KA case per 10,000 population at the sub-district level in Bangladesh and India, and at the district level in Nepal. Nepal has maintained this target for the past three years (since 2014), and other endemic countries in the region are nearing the achievement of this goal. To evaluate progress toward achieving the elimination target by Member States, a formal process must be established to validate the elimination of KA as a public health problem. This document outlines the process and steps that will be followed to validate the elimination of kala-azar as a public health problem.
